column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 34: “Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it”

column2: From Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand; if he is unable, then with his tongue; and if he is unable, then with his heart — and that is the weakest of faith.” Muslim reported it.

Muslim recorded this hadith through the narration of Qays ibn Muslim, from Ṭāriq ibn Shihāb, from Abū Saʿīd, and through the narration of Ismāʿīl ibn Rajāʾ, from his father, from Abū Saʿīd. In his version of Ṭāriq's hadith, Ṭāriq said:

The first to begin with the sermon before the prayer on the day of ʿĪd was Marwān. A man stood up to him and said: The prayer comes before the sermon. He said: What used to be done has been abandoned. Abū Saʿīd said: As for this man, he has done what was incumbent on him. Then he narrated this hadith.

Its meaning has also been narrated by other routes. Muslim recorded, from the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “There was no prophet whom Allah sent to a nation before me but he had from among his nation disciples and companions who took up his sunnah

and followed his command. Then after them came successors who say what they do not do and do what they are not commanded. Whoever strives against them with his hand is a believer, whoever strives against them with his tongue is a believer, and whoever strives against them with his heart is a believer; beyond that there is not so much as a mustard seed of faith.”
Sālim al-Murādī reported from ʿAmr ibn Harim, from Jābir ibn Zayd, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, that the Prophet ﷺ

said: “At the end of time my nation will be struck by a severe trial from its rulers. None will be saved from it except a man who knew the religion of Allah and stood by it with his tongue, his hand and his heart —
he is the one who has gone furthest ahead — and a man who knew the religion of Allah and affirmed it, though the first is ahead of him; and a man who knew the religion of Allah and kept silent:
if he saw someone doing good, he loved him for it, and if he saw someone doing falsehood, he hated him for it. That one will be saved despite his slowness.” This is unusual, and its chain is broken.
Al-Ismāʿīlī recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hārūn al-ʿAbdī — who is very weak — from a freed slave of ʿUmar, from ʿUmar, that the Prophet ﷺ

said: “This nation is close to perishing, except for three people: a man who rejected evil with his hand, his tongue and his heart; if he was too fearful to use his hand, then with his tongue and his heart; and if he was too fearful to use his tongue and his hand, then with his heart.”

He also recorded, through the narration of al-Awzāʿī, from ʿUmayr ibn Hāniʾ, from ʿAlī, that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say: “After me there will be trials in which the believer will be unable to change things with his hand or his tongue.” I said: Messenger of Allah, and how will that be?
He said: “They will reject it in their hearts.” I said: Messenger of Allah, will that diminish their faith at all?
He said: “No, except as the raindrop diminishes the smooth rock.” This chain is broken.
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded its meaning from the hadith of ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, from the Prophet ﷺ, with a weak chain.

All these hadiths show that rejecting evil is obligatory according to one's ability, and that rejecting it in the heart is indispensable: if someone's heart does not reject evil, that shows that faith has gone from his heart.

It has been narrated from Abū Juḥayfah, who said: ʿAlī said: The first jihād you will be overcome in is jihād with your hands, then jihād with your tongues, then jihād with your hearts. Whoever's heart does not recognise what is right and reject what is wrong is turned upside down, his top made his bottom.
Ibn Masʿūd heard a man say: Ruined is he who does not enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. Ibn Masʿūd said:

Ruined is he whose heart does not know what is right and what is wrong. He was pointing out that knowing right and wrong with the heart is an obligation from which no one is released; whoever does not know them is ruined.

Rejecting it with the tongue and the hand, however, is obligatory only according to one's capacity. Ibn Masʿūd said: Whoever of you lives long may well see an evil about which he can do nothing except that Allah knows from his heart that he hates it.

In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, from al-ʿUrs ibn ʿAmīrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “When a sin is committed on earth, whoever witnesses it and hates it is like one who was absent from it; and whoever is absent from it

but is pleased with it is like one who witnessed it.” So whoever witnesses a sin and hates it in his heart is like one who did not witness it, if he is unable to reject it with his tongue and his hand; and whoever is absent from it but is pleased with it is like one who witnessed it, was able to reject it, and did not;

because being pleased with sins is among the vilest of unlawful things, and through it one fails to reject the sin with the heart — an obligation on every Muslim from which no one is released in any circumstance.

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever is present at an act of disobedience and hates it is as though he were absent from it; and whoever is absent from it but loves it is as though he were present at it.” This is like the hadith before it.

It is clear from this that rejecting evil with the heart is an obligation on every Muslim in every circumstance, while rejecting it with the hand and the tongue depends on ability, as in the hadith of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet ﷺ, who said:

“There is no people among whom acts of disobedience are committed, who are able to change them and do not, but Allah is about to envelop them all in punishment.” Abū Dāwūd recorded it in this wording, and said: Shuʿbah said in it: “There is no people among whom acts of disobedience are committed, who are more numerous than those who commit them…”

He also recorded, from the hadith of Jarīr: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: “There is no man among a people who commits acts of disobedience among them, while they are able to stop him and do not, but Allah strikes them with punishment before they die.”

Imam Aḥmad recorded it, in this wording: “There is no people among whom acts of disobedience are committed, who are mightier and more numerous than those who commit them and do not change it, but Allah envelops them all in punishment.”
He also recorded, from the hadith of ʿAdī ibn ʿAmīrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:

“Allah does not punish the generality for the deeds of the few until they see evil in their midst, able to reject it, and do not reject it. When they do that, Allah punishes the few and the generality alike.”
He and Ibn Mājah also recorded, from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, who said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: “Allah will question the servant on the Day of Resurrection,
until He says: What prevented you, when you saw evil, from rejecting it? And when Allah prompts a servant with his argument, he will say: My Lord, I hoped in You, and I feared people.”
Then there is what al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded, also from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd, that the Prophet ﷺ said in his sermon:
“Let no man's awe of people prevent him from speaking the truth when he knows it.” Abū Saʿīd wept and said: By Allah, we have seen things and been overawed.
Imam Aḥmad recorded it with the addition: “For speaking the truth, or reminding people of something momentous, neither brings one's appointed time nearer nor puts one's provision further away.”

Likewise Imam Aḥmad and Ibn Mājah recorded, from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Let none of you belittle himself.” They said: Messenger of Allah, how would one of us belittle himself?

He said: “He sees a matter concerning Allah about which he ought to speak, and then does not speak about it. Allah will say to him on the Day of Resurrection: What prevented you from saying such-and-such concerning Me?
He will say: Fear of people. And Allah will say: It was I whom you had more right to fear.”
These two hadiths are to be understood as referring to the case where what keeps a person from rejecting evil is mere awe, not the kind of fear that releases him from the obligation to reject it.
Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: I said to Ibn ʿAbbās: Should I enjoin what is right on the ruler and forbid him what is wrong?

He said: If you fear that he will kill you, then no. I came back to it, and he told me the same; I came back to it again, and he told me the same, and said: If you must do it, then do it between yourself and him.
Ṭāwūs said: A man came to Ibn ʿAbbās and said: Shall I not stand up before this ruler and command him and forbid him?
He said: Do not become a trial for him. He said: What if he commands me to disobey Allah?
He said: That is the case you mean; then, be a man.

We have mentioned the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd which contains: “After them came successors… whoever strives against them with his hand is a believer…” and so on. This indicates striving against rulers with the hand.
Imam Aḥmad found this hadith objectionable, in the narration of Abū Dāwūd, saying: It goes against the hadiths in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded patience with the injustice of rulers.
It may be answered that changing evil with the hand does not entail fighting.

Aḥmad stated this explicitly too, in the narration of Ṣāliḥ, saying: Changing with the hand is not with the sword and weapons. Striving against rulers with the hand, then, means removing with one's own hand the evils they have committed, such as pouring away their wine or breaking their instruments of amusement and the like,
or annulling with one's hand the injustice they have ordered, if one has the power to do so. All of this is permissible; it is not a matter of fighting them,
nor of the rebellion against them that has been forbidden, for the most that is to be feared from it is that the one who enjoins is killed, alone.
Rebellion against them with the sword, however, is to be feared for the strife it brings, which leads to the shedding of Muslims' blood.

Admittedly, if in venturing to reject the evil of kings he fears that his family or neighbours will be harmed, he should not confront them in that case, because the harm would spread to others. So said al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ and others. Furthermore,

whenever he fears from them, for himself, the sword, the whip, prison, fetters, banishment, the seizure of his property or similar harm, the obligation to command and forbid them falls away. The imams have stated this explicitly, among them Mālik, Aḥmad, Isḥāq and others.
Aḥmad said: He is not to confront the ruler, for his sword is drawn.

Ibn Shubrumah said: Enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is like jihād: one man must hold firm against two, and fleeing from them is unlawful for him, but they are not obliged to hold firm against more than that.

If he fears abuse or hearing ugly words, he is not released from rejecting the evil because of that; Imam Aḥmad stated this explicitly. If he bears the harm and is strong enough for it, that is better; Aḥmad stated this too. It was said to him:
Has it not come from the Prophet ﷺ that he said, “It is not for the believer to humiliate himself” — that is, to expose himself to trials he cannot bear? He said: This is not of that kind.

What he said is supported by what Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Mājah and al-Tirmidhī recorded from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “The best jihād is a word of justice before a tyrannical ruler.”
Ibn Mājah recorded its meaning from the hadith of Abū Umāmah.
In the Musnad of al-Bazzār, with a chain that includes unknown narrators, from Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ, who said:
I said: Messenger of Allah, which of the martyrs is most honoured by Allah?
He said: “A man who stood up before a tyrannical ruler, enjoined on him what is right and forbade him what is wrong, and was killed by him.”
Its meaning has been narrated by other routes, all of them weak.
As for the hadith, “It is not fitting for the believer to humiliate himself,” it shows only that when he knows that he cannot bear the harm and will not endure it,

he should not then confront the one in authority; and this is true. The discussion concerns only one who knows himself to be capable of patience. So said the imams, such as Sufyān, Aḥmad, al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ and others.
Something has been narrated from Aḥmad indicating that rejecting evil in the heart is sufficient. He said, in the narration of Abū Dāwūd: We hope that if he rejects it in his heart,
he is safe, and if he rejects it with his hand, that is better. This is to be understood as applying when he is afraid, as he stated explicitly in the narration of more than one person.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā related two reported positions of Aḥmad on whether it is obligatory to reject evil when one knows that it will not be accepted, and he judged correct the view that it is obligatory. This is the view of most scholars.

One of the Salaf was asked about this, and said: It will be an excuse for you. This is like what Allah the Exalted tells of those who rejected the evil of the Sabbath-breakers, that when they were asked,

“‘Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?’ they said: ‘As an excuse before your Lord, and that perhaps they may fear Him’” [al-Aʿrāf 7:164]. But something has also been reported that can be taken as evidence that commanding and forbidding are no longer required when they are not accepted and bring no benefit.

In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, Ibn Mājah and al-Tirmidhī, from Abū Thaʿlabah al-Khushanī: he was asked: What do you say about this verse: “Upon you is [the care of] yourselves” [al-Māʾidah 5:105]? He said: By Allah, I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it,

and he said: “Rather, enjoin one another to what is right and forbid one another what is wrong, until, when you see avarice obeyed, desire followed, the world preferred, and everyone with an opinion delighted with his own opinion, then look to yourself and leave aside the affairs of the common people.”
In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, who said: While we were around the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he mentioned the time of trial,

and said: “When you see people whose covenants have fallen into confusion and whose trustworthiness has grown slight, and they are like this” — and he interlaced his fingers. I stood up to him and said: What should I do then, may Allah make me your ransom?
He said: “Keep to your house, control your tongue, take what you recognise and leave what you reject, and attend to your own particular affairs and leave aside the affairs of the common people.”

Likewise it is narrated from a group of the Companions concerning His words, Exalted is He: “Upon you is [the care of] yourselves; those who have gone astray will not harm you when you have been guided” [al-Māʾidah 5:105], that they said: The time for applying it has not yet come; it applies only at the end of time.

From Ibn Masʿūd, who said: When hearts and inclinations differ, and you are split into factions, and some of you taste the violence of others, then a person commands only himself; that is when this verse applies.
From Ibn ʿUmar, who said: This verse is for peoples who will come after us: if they speak, it will not be accepted from them.

Jubayr ibn Nufayr, reporting from a group of the Companions, said that they said: When you see avarice obeyed, desire followed, and everyone with an opinion delighted with his own opinion, then look to yourself: whoever has gone astray will not harm you when you have been guided.

From Makḥūl, who said: The time for applying it has not yet come. When the admonisher is overawed and the one admonished rejects the admonition, then look to yourself: whoever has gone astray will not harm you when you have been guided.
From al-Ḥasan: whenever he recited this verse, he would say: What an assurance it is, and how sure!
And what latitude, and how wide!
All this may be taken to mean that whoever is unable to enjoin what is right, or fears harm, is released from it. Ibn ʿUmar's words show that whoever knows that it will not be accepted from him
is not obliged to do it, as is related as a reported position of Aḥmad. Al-Awzāʿī likewise said: Command those you think will accept it from you.
His words ﷺ about the one who rejects evil in his heart, “and that is the weakest of faith,” show that enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong are among the traits of faith.
They also show that whoever is able to carry out one of the traits of faith and does so is better than one who leaves it because he is unable. This is further shown by his words ﷺ about women:

“As for the deficiency in her religion, she remains days and nights without praying” — referring to the days of menstruation — even though she is forbidden to pray at that time; and he counted that as a deficiency in her religion.
This shows that whoever is able to carry out an obligation and does it is better than one who is unable and leaves it, even if he is excused for leaving it. And Allah knows best.
His words ﷺ, “Whoever among you sees an evil,” show that rejection is tied to seeing. If the evil is concealed and he has not seen it,
but knows of it, then Aḥmad's explicit position in most narrations is that he does not interfere with it, and does not search out what he has misgivings about.

Another reported position of his is that he uncovers what is hidden if he is certain of it. If he hears the sound of unlawful singing or of instruments of amusement and knows the place where they are,
he rejects it, because he is certain of the evil and knows where it is, so it is as if he had seen it. Aḥmad stated this explicitly, saying: If he does not know where it is, he has no obligation.

As for climbing over walls to get at people one knows to have gathered for some evil, the imams, such as Sufyān al-Thawrī and others, rejected it; it falls under the spying that has been forbidden. It was said to Ibn Masʿūd: So-and-so's beard is dripping with wine. He said: Allah has forbidden us to spy.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā said in his book al-Aḥkām al-Sulṭāniyyah: If the evil that he thinks most likely is being committed in secret, on a trustworthy person's report, involves a violation of sanctity that cannot afterwards be remedied, such as fornication or killing,

then spying and venturing to uncover and investigate it are permissible, for fear of letting slip a violation of what is sacred that cannot be remedied. If it is of a lesser degree than that, spying on it and uncovering it are not permissible.

The evil that must be rejected is what is agreed upon. As for what is disputed, some of the scholars of our [Ḥanbalī] school said that it need not be rejected in someone who does it by his own ijtihād, or by following a mujtahid in a way that is permissible.

Al-Qāḍī, in al-Aḥkām al-Sulṭāniyyah, made an exception for matters in which the disagreement is weak and which are a means to something prohibited by agreement: for example, usury in spot exchange, over which the disagreement is weak and which is a means to usury through delay (ribā al-nasāʾ), whose prohibition is agreed upon; and temporary marriage (mutʿah), which is a means to fornication.
He mentioned that Abū Isḥāq ibn Shāqlā stated that mutʿah is outright fornication.
It is reported from Ibn Baṭṭah that he said: A marriage that a judge has ruled valid is not annulled if he based his ruling on some interpretation,

unless he ruled in a man's favour on a contract of mutʿah, or ruled that a man who pronounced three divorces in a single utterance may take his wife back without her first marrying another husband: such a ruling is rejected, and the one who made it deserves punishment and an exemplary penalty.

Aḥmad's explicit position is that one who plays chess is to be rebuked, and al-Qāḍī interpreted this as referring to one who plays it without ijtihād or permissible following. This is open to question, for Aḥmad's explicit position is that one who drinks nabīdh, over which there is disagreement, receives the prescribed punishment,

and carrying out the prescribed punishment is the most severe degree of rejection; yet in his view the drinker does not become a sinner (fāsiq) by it. This shows that everything disputed is to be rejected when the disagreement over it is weak, because the Sunnah indicates that it is unlawful, while one who does it on the basis of an interpretation is not thereby stripped of probity. And Allah knows best.

Aḥmad likewise stated explicitly that one who does not complete his prayer, and does not straighten his back after bowing and prostration, is to be rebuked, even though there is disagreement over whether that is obligatory.

Know that a person is moved to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong sometimes by hope of its reward; sometimes by fear of punishment for neglecting it; sometimes by anger for Allah's sake at the violation of what He has made sacred;

sometimes by sincere counsel for the believers and mercy towards them, and the hope of rescuing them from what they have thrown themselves into, exposing themselves to Allah's anger and punishment in this world and the Hereafter;

and sometimes by reverence for Allah, glorifying Him and loving Him, and the knowledge that He deserves to be obeyed and not disobeyed, remembered and not forgotten, thanked and not met with ingratitude,

and that lives and wealth should be given as ransom against the violation of what He has made sacred. As one of the Salaf said: I would love it if all creation obeyed Allah, even if my flesh were cut up with shears.

ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (may Allah have mercy on them both) used to say to his father: I would love it if the cooking pots boiled with me and you, for the sake of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Whoever keeps this station and the one before it in view will find light all the harm he meets for the sake of Allah the Exalted, and he may even pray for those who harm him,
as the Prophet ﷺ did when his people struck him and he began wiping the blood from his face, saying: “My Lord, forgive my people, for they do not know.”
In every case, gentleness in rejecting evil is essential. Sufyān al-Thawrī said: None should enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong except one who has three traits:
gentle in what he enjoins, gentle in what he forbids; just in what he enjoins, just in what he forbids; knowledgeable about what he enjoins, knowledgeable about what he forbids.

Aḥmad said: People need tact and gentleness — enjoining what is right without harshness — except for a man who openly flaunts his sinfulness, for he has no sanctity. He said: When Ibn Masʿūd's companions passed people in whom they saw something they disliked, they would say: Gently, may Allah have mercy on you! Gently, may Allah have mercy on you!
Aḥmad said: He should enjoin with gentleness and humility. If they say to him things he dislikes, he should not become angry, or he will be seeking to avenge himself.
